title: The snowbirds are flying in from the north woods
body: Juncos are leaving spruce forests in Canada, where the first frost has already silvered the moss. They fly by night, cold air streaming over their gray backs, and land by morning in the hedges {where}.

weatherNote.wind: Tonight's north wind is exactly what they wait for. Travelers pour south on the back of a cold front, thousands at a time, in the dark.
weatherNote.rain: Rain grounds travelers overnight, so after a wet night the parks can fill with tired, hungry birds, resting before they go on.
weatherNote.fog: In fog, migrants fly low and sometimes land to wait it out. Listen for thin calls overhead.
weatherNote.cold: A cold snap up north pushes even more of them down toward us.

title: White-throats are dropping into the leaf piles
body: A week ago they were in quiet northern bogs, singing over still water. Now they're scratching through crunchy leaves {where}, still whistling their song from up there: oh sweet Canada, Canada.

title: The brant are coming home from the Arctic
body: These little sea geese spent the summer on tundra where the sun never set. They've flown thousands of miles over cold gray ocean, and now they're bobbing in the harbor, smelling of salt and eelgrass.

title: Butter butts are pouring down the coast
body: Yellow-rumped warblers are leaving dark evergreen forests up north, riding the cold fronts down the shoreline. They'll stay all winter, living on waxy bayberries {where}.

title: The chimney swifts are heading for the Amazon
body: The little birds who twittered over the rooftops all summer are flying to the warm, humid rivers of Peru, thousands of miles south. They'll eat bugs on the wing the whole way and won't land on a branch once.

weatherNote.wind: A north wind like today's carries them south fast, tiny cigars riding the gusts.

title: The monarchs are floating south to Mexico
body: Each one is headed for the same cool mountain forests their great-great-grandparents left in spring, a place they've never seen. They glide on warm afternoon air, sipping goldenrod and asters {where} along the way.

weatherNote.wind: On a north wind, monarchs ride the breeze south and barely flap at all.
weatherNote.rain: In rain they hang under leaves, wings folded, waiting for the sun to warm them up again.
weatherNote.cold: Cold mornings keep them still until the sun warms their wings.

title: The catbirds are going to the Caribbean
body: After a summer of berries and meowing from the bushes {where}, catbirds are flying south to Florida, Cuba and Central America, where it smells like warm rain and flowers. The thickets will be quieter until May.

weatherNote.wind: They'll take off on a north wind tonight, flying in the dark.

title: The terns are flying to South American beaches
body: The sharp-winged birds who dove for silver fish in the harbor all summer are heading down the coast to warm surf in Brazil and Argentina. Their kids are going too, on their first big trip.

title: Gulls from the far north are riding in on the cold
body: When northern lakes and bays freeze, gulls drift south to our open water. Look for big mixed crowds on piers and ice edges, standing in the wind like they've done this forever (they have).

weatherNote.cold: Today's cold up north is sending more of them our way.
weatherNote.snow: Snow up north means fresh arrivals here, looking for open water.
weatherNote.wind: They ride the cold winds down the coast.

title: Buffleheads have settled in on the open water
body: These tiny ducks raised their families in old woodpecker holes by northern lakes. Now those lakes are frozen solid, and they're bobbing and diving here, where the water stays open.

weatherNote.cold: The colder it gets up north, the more of them arrive.
weatherNote.snow: The snow falling here is already ice and silence up where they came from.

title: A few hermit thrushes decided to stay
body: Most hermit thrushes are in the warm south now, but a few tough ones are spending winter in thickets {where}, living on berries, quiet as snowfall.

weatherNote.snow: On snowy days they tuck under the thickest bushes, out of the wind.

title: The monarchs are asleep on a mountain in Mexico
body: The butterflies who drifted past in fall are clustered by the millions on fir trees high in the mountains, so many that branches bend. When the sun warms them, the air fills with orange wings.

title: The chimney swifts are in the Amazon
body: While we're bundled up, the swifts are zipping over warm rivers in Peru, chasing bugs in the humid air. In spring they'll fly all the way back to the same chimneys.

title: The catbirds are meowing somewhere warm
body: Right now they're in sunny gardens in Florida and the Caribbean, eating fruit and meowing from different bushes. Their hedges {where} are waiting for them.

title: The chimney swifts are back from the Amazon
body: They flew up from warm South American rivers, crossing the Gulf of Mexico in the dark, eating bugs on the wing the whole way. Look up for cigar-shaped birds twittering over the rooftops {where}.

weatherNote.wind: A warm south wind tonight is a highway north. Travelers ride it through the dark, high above the streetlights.
weatherNote.rain: Rain can stop travelers overnight, and the next morning the trees can be full of birds who weren't there yesterday.
weatherNote.fog: In fog, birds on the move fly lower. Some land to wait for the sky to clear.

title: The red-winged blackbirds are first back to the marsh
body: The males arrive while it's still cold, from farm fields down south, and grab the best cattails. Conk-la-ree! They're flashing their red shoulders before the reeds have even turned green.

title: The catbirds are back from the Caribbean
body: A week ago they were meowing in warm gardens in Cuba and Central America. Now they're back in the bushes {where}, meowing in the cool spring air like they never left.

weatherNote.wind: A warm south wind tonight is a highway north. Travelers ride it through the dark, high above the streetlights.
weatherNote.rain: Rain can stop travelers overnight, and the next morning the trees can be full of birds who weren't there yesterday.

title: The terns are back from South America
body: They've flown up the whole coast of two continents, following the warm water. Now they're diving for fish in the harbor, calling kee-arr! into the salt wind.

weatherNote.wind: A warm south wind tonight is a highway north. Travelers ride it through the dark, high above the streetlights.

title: The snowbirds are flying home to the north woods
body: The little gray birds who spent winter under your hedges are flying back to spruce forests in Canada, where the snow is just melting and the air smells like pine.

weatherNote.wind: A south wind tonight will carry them north fast.

title: The brant are flying back to the Arctic
body: These little sea geese are heading for tundra at the top of the world, where the sun will soon never set and the ground is just thawing. They'll nest by icy ponds and come back in fall with their kids.

weatherNote.wind: They wait for a good south wind to make the long flight easier.

title: The white-throats are singing their way north
body: They're heading to quiet northern bogs and forests, still whistling oh sweet Canada as they go. The leaf piles {where} will be a little quieter.

title: The monarchs made it back north
body: These are the great-great-grandchildren of last fall's travelers, born along the way on milkweed in Texas and beyond. They've floated north on warm breezes, and they're laying eggs on the milkweed {where}.

weatherNote.heat: Hot days are perfect monarch weather. They sip nectar and glide on the warm air.

title: The fireflies are rising from the grass
body: They spent almost two years underground as glowing larvae, hunting slugs in the damp dark. Now, on warm humid nights, they're climbing up the grass blades and taking off, blinking.

weatherNote.heat: Warm, sticky evenings like this one are when they flash the most.
weatherNote.rain: After the rain clears, the damp air brings them out in force.

title: The dragonflies are climbing out of the pond
body: Blue dashers lived underwater as nymphs for months. Now they're crawling up reeds, splitting their old skin, and drying shiny new wings in the warm sun.

weatherNote.heat: Heat makes them fast. On days like this they zip and dart all afternoon.

title: The baby birds are moving out
body: Young robins, sparrows and starlings are leaving their parents' care, spotty and clumsy, figuring out the world on their own. By fall you won't be able to tell them from the grown-ups.

title: The swifts are gathering for the big trip
body: In late summer, chimney swifts gather by the hundreds at dusk and swirl down into one big chimney together, like smoke in reverse. They're getting ready for the long flight to the Amazon.
